transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah… I guess what finally made me come in is that I’ve just sort of stopped caring about the things that usually keep me steady. Like, I used to look forward to sailing races—there’s this whole routine with checking the lines and the weather, and half the guys argue about wind direction like it’s a Supreme Court case—but now it just feels like another obligation.

Same with my Saturday shift at the historical society. I used to enjoy it, talking to people, organizing old records, that kind of thing. Even my woodshop stuff… I’ll walk in there, look at a project, and just turn around. It all feels like chores I keep putting off, and that’s not really like me.
Have you noticed feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, lately?

I don’t know if I’d call it “depressed” exactly… it’s more like this low-grade dread that’s just kind of there most days. And guilt. Like I keep replaying things and thinking I should’ve seen one more risk coming, even though people keep telling me the controls were in place.

It’s funny—well, not funny—but in project management you spend so much time trying to anticipate every possible failure point. I used to be the guy with the contingency plan for the contingency plan. And now that same habit just sort of follows me around in my head, like I missed something obvious. So yeah, most days there’s this weight to it.
Have you noticed feeling fatigued or having low energy most days, even when you haven’t been physically active?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, I get tired like anyone does, but I haven’t really been tracking whether it’s most days or not. Some days I’ll sit down after work and feel kind of spent, but then again my work has always had a lot of mental juggling—budgets, schedules, people needing answers yesterday.

It’s like when we were coordinating a marina renovation years back, everyone thought the physical labor was the hard part, but half the exhaustion was just keeping the moving pieces from colliding. So… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly noticed low energy even when I haven’t done anything. Not in a way I can pin down.
Have you found it harder to focus on tasks, make decisions, or think clearly lately?

I’m not sure I can say that’s been a clear thing. I mean, I make decisions all day for work, so sometimes by the end of it I don’t want to decide what to have for dinner, but that’s not exactly new.

Focus… I don’t know. I’ll read the same email twice sometimes, but I’ve done that for years when there are too many moving parts. It’s like when you’re managing a schedule and one subcontractor being late makes three other things slide—your brain starts hopping tracks. Sorry, that’s probably not what you’re asking.

I guess I haven’t noticed a big change in thinking clearly or anything I could point to and say, “Yeah, that’s new.”
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or on the flip side, feeling restless or fidgety lately?

I don’t think so… not that I’ve noticed. I mean, I’m not pacing around the room or anything, and nobody’s told me I’m talking slower.

Sometimes I’ll tap a pen in meetings, but I’ve always done that—drove one of my old supervisors nuts, actually. He used to take the pen right out of my hand during budget reviews because I’d be clicking it while we were going through cost lines. But that’s not really new, I don’t think.

So… no clear change that I can point to.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight lately—like eating a lot more or a lot less than usual?

Not really, no. I mean, my weight sort of moves around a few pounds depending on the week, but I haven’t noticed anything dramatic.

Appetite-wise… I still eat. Some days I’ll skip lunch if meetings run long, but that’s always been the case in project work. You get on a call about permitting or vendor timelines and suddenly it’s 2:30 and you’re eating a granola bar from your desk drawer. But I wouldn’t say I’m eating a lot more or a lot less than usual. Nothing that really stands out.
Have you found yourself thinking about death or suicide lately?

No… I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve thought about death in the general way people do, I guess—like when someone in the news passes away, or you hear about an accident on the highway and it sticks with you for a minute.

Actually, there was this guy I used to work with who had a whole lecture about driving defensively near construction zones, and now every time traffic narrows down to one lane I think about that. But, sorry—that’s not really what you asked.

No, I haven’t been thinking about killing myself or anything like that.
Would you say that most days feel emotionally worse than they used to, even if it's not a sharp sadness—like a general, ongoing low mood?

Yeah… I think that’s fair. It’s not like I wake up crying or anything, but most days there’s this… low-grade dread, I guess. Like something’s going to be missed, or I should’ve caught one more thing.

And guilt, too. That’s probably the bigger piece. People keep telling me the controls were in place, that the risks were reviewed, all of that. I mean, in project management you live in risk registers and mitigation plans—half my job is asking, “What are we not seeing?” I used to have this manager who’d say, “If it isn’t documented, it didn’t happen,” which was annoying but also kind of true.

Sorry, I’m getting off track. But yes… emotionally, most days feel heavier than they used to. Not sharp sadness exactly. More like that dread and guilt just follows me around.
Would you say that you've been feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, for the past two weeks or more?

Yeah… I mean, “depressed” is a word I’m never sure fits exactly. It’s more like this low-grade dread and guilt that’s there most days, like I should’ve seen one more risk coming or caught something earlier.

People keep telling me the controls were in place, that it wasn’t just on me, and I know—on paper, I know how that works. We had reviews, sign-offs, the whole chain. I’ve spent years in project work where you’re supposed to think three steps ahead, and sometimes I still find myself mentally going back through it like it’s one of those post-project lessons learned meetings that never ends.

So… yes, most days have felt pretty down, or heavy, for a while now. Not necessarily crying-all-day depressed, but that dread and guilt follows me around.
Have you noticed a loss of pleasure or interest in activities that you used to enjoy, like sailing races, your historical society shift, or your woodshop projects?

Yeah… that’s actually part of why I finally agreed to come in. Those were the things that usually kept me level, you know? The sailing races, my Saturday shift at the historical society, messing around in the woodshop.

I used to look forward to that stuff. I mean, the woodshop especially—there’s something about sanding a piece properly, getting the edge right… I had this old neighbor who could tell what kind of finish someone used from across the room, which was ridiculous, but he was usually right.

But lately it all just feels like chores. I keep putting it off. Even the things I know I used to enjoy, I just… don’t really care about them the same way.
How long have you been feeling this way—this low mood, loss of interest, and the feelings of dread and guilt?

It’s been… a little over a year now, I think. Since the scaffold accident, during that whole business readjustment period.

I keep measuring time around that, which I hate. Before that, after that. There were all these meetings then—staffing changes, budget reviews, trying to keep projects moving—and I remember thinking we just had to get through the transition. But then the accident happened, and… yeah. Since then, this low feeling and the guilt have just kind of stayed with me.
Have you noticed your mood getting significantly worse at any point, to the point where you felt barely able to function or where even small tasks felt almost impossible to complete?

Not completely unable to function, no… I’m still working, still showing up. I don’t want to make it sound like I’ve collapsed or anything.

But it has gotten worse in a practical way. I’ve started handing off site visits that I really should be leading myself. And if there’s a client discussion where the accident might come up, I’ll find some reason to let someone else take it. Which—honestly, in project work, that’s not nothing. Direction matters. People take their cues from you.

It reminds me of this one job years ago where the whole schedule went sideways just because nobody wanted to own the uncomfortable meeting—sorry, that’s not exactly what you asked. But, yeah… small tasks aren’t impossible, exactly. It’s more that certain parts of the job feel like I’m walking right up to a live wire, so I avoid them. And then I worry I’m not giving the project the steady hand it needs.
